question.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).$ 

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

where ${u}_{1}={u}_{1}(x),{u}_{2}={u}_{2}(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x,$ we obtain

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have the following constraint equation relating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}:$

$$
{{field-4}}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-3{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-3{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-3{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & =3{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-3{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\cancel{3{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\cancel{3{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} & =\cancel{3{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}-\cancel{3{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=0.
$$
